query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an ultrathin molybdenum interlayer onto the tungsten surfaces before the formation of the composite can suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation during subsequent heat‐transfer and irradiation exposure, thereby enhancing the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite in which tungsten exists as discrete particles or an interconnected ligament network embedded within a copper matrix that, under operational thermal cycling and irradiation conditions, exhibits phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.intervention: A one‐step, pre‐assembly deposit of an ultrathin (on the order of a few nanometers) molybdenum (Mo) interlayer on the tungsten surfaces.
generation.conditions: This intervention is implemented before composite assembly, with the composite subsequently undergoing standard processing and exposure to elevated heat-transfer and irradiation conditions typical for joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo interlayer creates a chemically graded interface that bonds well with both tungsten and copper, reducing the interfacial energy and promoting a coherent, continuous phase across the interface.
generation.mechanism: Mo is known to have good wetting behavior with both tungsten and copper. Its presence at the interface can enhance atomic diffusion and bonding during heat treatment, reducing the thermodynamic driving force for Cu dewetting and phase separation. Under irradiation, the Mo layer is expected to help fill developing voids, thus maintaining a continuous thermal path and preventing the formation of interfacial defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-interlayer-treated composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids and reduced phase separation, resulting in an improved and more stable thermal conductivity compared to untreated composites under similar heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite with its conventional W–Cu interface exhibits phase separation and void formation that undermine thermal transport and long-term reliability under demanding thermal/irradiation environments.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to W–Cu composites used in plasma-facing or cooling component joints where the operational temperature and irradiation environments are similar to those simulated in accelerated aging tests. The optimum interlayer thickness and processing conditions may require further tuning within these application limits.
generation.uncertainty: While Mo is chosen for its interfacial and wetting properties, the exact interlayer thickness and its long-term stability under irradiation conditions remain to be optimized. The optimal processing route and the quantitative effect on thermal conductivity are yet to be experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set where tungsten surfaces are pre-coated with an ultrathin Mo interlayer (using a technique such as sputtering or atomic layer deposition) and a control set without the coating. Subject both sets to accelerated thermal cycling and controlled irradiation (e.g., ion-beam irradiation simulating the operational environment).
measurements: Characterization of the interfacial structure via high-resolution TEM and EDS to assess void formation and phase homogeneity
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., using laser flash analysis) before and after accelerated aging/irradiation
XRD analysis for phase identification and detection of phase separation
Mechanical tests to assess the integrity of the interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-interlayer treated composites do not show statistically significant improvements in interfacial integrity (i.e., reduced or absent voids and phase separation) and thermal conductivity relative to the untreated controls under identical aging and irradiation conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
